# RHTAS Build Process

This part of the document will highlight the necessary steps to produce a build for RHTAS Operator. This does not include MVO or PCO. Tooling

## Tas Operator Dependencies

A single build of Tas Operator as of 1.4 is dependent on the following Konflux Applications in our Konflux Cluster. Each Konflux App is linked please investigate them yourself.

* [Tas-Components](https://konflux-ui.apps.stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1.openshiftapps.com/ns/rhtas-tenant/applications/tas-components/components) (Branch)  
  * Trillian logserver  
  * Trillian logsigner  
  * Trillian Database  
  * Rekor-Backfill-redis  
  * Rekor Server  
  * Fulcio Server  
  * Trillian-redis  
  * certificate-transparency-go  
  * Rekor-Search-UI  
  * Timestamp-Authority  
* [Tas-Tools](https://konflux-ui.apps.stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1.openshiftapps.com/ns/rhtas-tenant/applications/tas-tools/) (Branch)  
  * Cosign  
  * Gitsign  
  * Rekor-cli  
  * Fetch-tsa-certs  
  * Update-tree  
* [Client-Server](https://konflux-ui.apps.stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1.openshiftapps.com/ns/rhtas-tenant/applications/client-server/components) (Branch)  
  * Client-Server  
* [Rekor-Monitor](https://konflux-ui.apps.stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1.openshiftapps.com/ns/rhtas-tenant/applications/rekor-monitor/components) (Branch)  
  * Rekor-Monitor  
  * Ctlog-monitor  
* [Create-Tree](https://konflux-ui.apps.stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1.openshiftapps.com/ns/rhtas-tenant/applications/create-tree/components) (Branch)  
  * Create-tree  
* [Tough](https://konflux-ui.apps.stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1.openshiftapps.com/ns/rhtas-tenant/applications/tough/components) (Branch)  
  * Tuf-tool  
  * Tuffer

Upon any of the subcomponents of each group successfully completing an on push build pipeline run 3 things happen. 

1. The first is that a snapshot is created. A snapshot is an object created by the konflux that contains all of the most recent successful builds of all of its components.  For further insight on snapshots see [here](https://konflux-ci.dev/docs/testing/integration/snapshots/).  
2. The second thing to occur is nudging  
   1. When a snapshot is created successfully konflux will send out a pr to another repo assuming its nudging relationship is configured. For more info on nudging see [here](http://konflux-ci.dev/docs/building/component-nudges/).  
   2. An example for nudging would be a successful build of fulcio leads to konflux opening a pr against our secure-sign-operator repo updating the operator to use the newly built fulcio image.  
3. The third thing to happen is our “Promote to candidate” pipeline is run after the snapshots creation. This pushes snapshot data to the bot branches within the release repo. [Link to bot branch](https://github.com/securesign/releases/tree/RHTAS-build-bot_candidate-images-main)

## Tas Dependency Builds

Before building the Tas Operator we must ensure we have fresh builds of the dependencies. It is important to clarify now we are talking about “on-push” builds, these are triggered via the ui or by merging a pr into the relevant onboarded branch in Github. 

For the sake of keeping this straightforward we will produce the container builds via the ui.  
Within any of the relevant Applications navigate to the components tab and click on the drop down near “Build Logs” on one of the components entries.  
![][image1]  
Selecting “Start New Build”  will trigger a new build off the most recent commit within the targeted branch. Alternatively there will likely be dependency update or go base image pull requests from mintmaker. If tests are passing those can be merged to generate the builds. Trigger builds for all of the above components except for Client Server. Build times can vary between 5 minutes and 20 minutes. You can monitor the build pipelines in the activity tab. As Builds succeed nudge pull requests will begin to open in secure-sign-operator repo and within the cosign repo.   
When all containers are built proceed to the cosign repo and merge the open nudge requests for the client-server.

### Client-Server

Client Server is the sensitive part of the build as we need the images within it to align with the snapshot for Tas-Tools, Tough and Create-tree. If the images present do not align with the targeted snapshots this can result in the need for a rebuild so it is important to check and verify.  
Note: Client Server will hopefully be gone by 1.5 but step remains relevant for z-stream release of prior TAS Versions.

## Operator Build

Assuming all container builds mentioned above are complete there will be a large amount of konflux nudge pr’s to update the images. You can merge them one by one or combine them into one custom pr (Usually the better option).  Once a pr is prepared this is usually a good point to verify that everything is aligned in terms of snapshots. Operator build will finish in 10 minutes but e2e tests will take from 30 minutes to an hour. Once merged the Operator Snapshot will be pushed to [bot branch](https://github.com/securesign/releases/tree/RHTAS-build-bot_candidate-images-main) after the success of the on-push pipelines. With that Operator Snapshot grab the image address for the operator-bundle we will need it to begin the FBC builds.

## FBC Build

To begin the FBC builds go to the FBC repo within the Securesign Github org. Navigate to the actions tab and select “Create New Release Items for FBC Catalog” action and fill out the relevant information.  
Some Important Notes

* Be sure to name the branch after the current release  
* Ensure the correct OCP Versions are added to the OCP field. Different Versions of Tas Support different OCP versions  
* Ensure the correct stable channels are selected for the operator.  
* When swapping the bundle image reference, keep the registry address but swap out the actual sha256.  
  * We use mirroring in our tests which allows us to have that in place.  
* Ensure you are pointing at the correct directory for Build  
  * As of writing this MVO and PCO have yet to be onboarded to using this action for build generation and are done manually.

Once the PR is created FBC builds will run followed by a lot of e2e tests related to the OCP versions.  
![][image2]

# Release Candidate Curation

## Release Candidate Curation

This is where we collect all of the snapshots for the current release of RHTAS and create the relevant ReleasePlans. This can be generated via an action (Which is in need of an update as of the 15th of April 2026). Or by copying the previous release directory and updating the info to match that of the current related snapshots which can be sourced either from konflux or the bot branch mentioned in earlier sections. 

I will now dive into the individual directories of a Release-Candidate directory. In this instance I will use [1.3.3](https://github.com/securesign/releases/tree/main/1.3.3/stable) as an example. Within any of our release directories we have several sub directories and a snapshot.json file. But before we talk about that we should highlight that the core part of us being able to release is having the relevant Release Plan Admission (RPA) prepared up on Konflux Release Data on [gitlab](https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/releng/konflux-release-data/-/blob/main/config/stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1/product/ReleasePlanAdmission/rhtas/stack-v1-3.yaml?ref_type=heads). 

## Release Plan Admission

The RPA is where we map our components/quay images to their registry counterparts. This is also assuming the relevant registry entry has been created within comet (see the comet section for more info). Another important piece of data within the RPA itself is the tag. When we release the images will be tagged with whatever version is present within the RPA. RPA are ideally created well in advance of releases but should always be verified as a part of the Release Candidate Verification Process. For extra information on RPA refer to the konflux [docs](https://konflux-ci.dev/docs/releasing/create-release-plan-admission/).

## 

## Release Plan

Release Plans contain our release notes and point to both a staging and production RPA. See example [here](https://github.com/securesign/releases/blob/main/1.3.3/stable/releasePlans/components/client-server-v1-3.yaml). These can be seen within the metadata under labels

```
apiVersion: appstudio.redhat.com/v1alpha1
kind: ReleasePlan
metadata:
  labels:
    release.appstudio.openshift.io/auto-release: "false"
    release.appstudio.openshift.io/releasePlanAdmission: stack-v1-3
    release.appstudio.openshift.io/standing-attribution: "true"
    release.rhtas.stage/releasePlanAdmission: rhtas-staging-v1-3
  name: create-tree-v1-3-1-3-3
  namespace: rhtas-tenant
spec:
  data:
    releaseNotes:
      type: "RHSA"
      synopsis: "RHTAS 1.3.3 - Red Hat Trusted Artifact Signer Release"
      topic: <Release notes featuring links to TAS docs and supported OCP versions>
      cves:
        - key: CVE-2025-61726
          component: create-tree-v1-3
        - key: CVE-2025-61728
          component: create-tree-v1-3
```

 Under the release notes section the following should be noted.

* Type  
  * Usually either RHEA or RHSA  
    * Difference being RHSA is when CVE fixes are present and RHEA when it is just a general release.  
    * RHSA requires cves: to be present within the release notes section.  
    * These require the cve id and the component that features the fix.  
* Metadata labels  
  * Ensuring the autorelease is set to false is important.  
  * Ensuring both staging and prod releasePlanAdmissions point to the correct RPA.

## Release Objects

```
apiVersion: appstudio.redhat.com/v1alpha1
kind: Release
metadata:
  name: client-server-v1-3-1-3-3
  namespace: rhtas-tenant
spec:
  releasePlan: client-server-v1-3-1-3-3
  snapshot: client-server-v1-3-20260312-102637-000

```

This is an example of a release snapshot. The info to note here is mostly the releasePlan and snapshot info in the spec. The ReleasePlan should align with the name of the corresponding releaseplan and the snapshot should align with whatever snapshot is in snapshot.json

## snapshot.json

All of the snapshots related to whatever is intended to be released is located here. This file doesn't need too much explaining. But it is important to note that any updates to the snapshots in this file means that the snapshots within the related release object should also be updated.

## Structural Tests and Other Checks

After creating the branch and opening a pull request against main several checks will run. Ideally all of these should pass before being handed over for testing.

### Konflux Integration Test Gate

This check ensures that all of the snapshots we are hoping to use in the release have all their Konflux Integration Tests passing. If any need to be retriggered this action will fail and produce logs telling which snapshot needs integration tests to be rerun. To retrigger these you can locate the snapshot within the ui and retrigger the particular Integration Scenario.

### RHTAS Staging

This attempts to run a staging release of resources by swapping out certain info within the release resources themselves. It allows for us to do an automated dry run for the release itself. It is worth noting that there can be failure due to high traffic, but it is always worth checking as this can catch anything that might be misconfigured.

### Structural Test \- Acceptance

These check if all the images present within snapshots.json align, comparing images present within operator snapshots to that of the FBC catalogs etc. The structural tests are modular and parts can be configured as needs be. See [here](https://github.com/securesign/releases/blob/main/1.3.3/stable/testingResources/structural-tests.yaml) for an example of configuring the structural tests. For code changes needed in the structural tests see the structural tests repo on github.

### Structural Tests \- Check Resources

This test is straightforward, it simply checks that the snapshots in snapshot.json align with the ones present within the release resources of the branch.

### Handover

Assuming that all tests have passed on this PR it is ready for handover. A jira is then created for testing, see [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/SECURESIGN-4270](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/SECURESIGN-4270) as example. Once all these JIRAS have been tested and no issues have been found. Sign off is provided.

### Running Release

After receiving a signoff release is run manually. First the engineer will log into the konflux cluster using this command. Note this will prompt log in via browser.

```
oc login --web https://api.stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1.openshiftapps.com:6443/
```

Following this they will verify they are with the rhtas-tenant namespace.

```
oc project rhtas-tenant
```

Once logged into our namespace within the cluster. We then apply all of the ReleasePlan Resources within our directory.

```
oc apply -f 1.3.3/stable/releasePlans/<grouping>/<release-plan>.yaml
```

Once the release plans have been applied to the cluster we then would apply the release objects. These should be done in the order of components, operator then fbc, once a release resource has been applied it will become visible within the release tab of the related konflux application.  
![][image3]    
Upon a release failing the release pipeline should be investigated. If it proves to just be a timeout or some transient error with Konflux feel free to delete the release resource and reapply to retrigger the release.

# PCO

## Policy Controller Operator Build Process

### **Overview**

The build process for the Policy Controller Operator (PCO) follows a similar pattern to the RHTAS and MVO operators, build the policy controller image, update the reference in the operator, then generate the File-Based Catalogs (FBCs) for the new build.

Unlike RHTAS, the PCO build process is currently **manual**. While nudging has been configured, Konflux limitations require manually retrieving the policy controller image, opening a PR to update the digest, merging, and then handling the FBCs separately. The PCO has not yet been onboarded to the same automated FBC workflow as RHTAS.

### **Konflux Applications**

We maintain three parallel sets of applications in Konflux, one per release stream:

| Stream | Policy Controller | Policy Controller Operator | Branch |
| :---- | :---: | :---: | :---- |
| tech-preview | [Application link](https://konflux-ui.apps.stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1.openshiftapps.com/ns/rhtas-tenant/applications/policy-controller-tech-preview) | [Application link](https://konflux-ui.apps.stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1.openshiftapps.com/ns/rhtas-tenant/applications/policy-controller-operator-tech-preview) | [Branch Link](https://github.com/securesign/policy-controller/tree/tech-preview) |
| main | [Application link](https://konflux-ui.apps.stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1.openshiftapps.com/ns/rhtas-tenant/applications/policy-controller) | [Application link](https://konflux-ui.apps.stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1.openshiftapps.com/ns/rhtas-tenant/applications/policy-controller-operator) | [Branch Link](https://github.com/securesign/policy-controller/tree/main) |
| 1.0 | [Application link](https://konflux-ui.apps.stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1.openshiftapps.com/ns/rhtas-tenant/applications/policy-controller-v1-0) | [Application link](https://konflux-ui.apps.stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1.openshiftapps.com/ns/rhtas-tenant/applications/policy-controller-operator-v1-0) | [Branch Link](https://github.com/securesign/policy-controller/tree/release-1.0) |

Each operator application mirrors its corresponding policy controller application.

### **Build Steps**

1. **Build the policy controller** \- Trigger and retrieve a build of the policy controller for the target stream using konflux.  
2. **Update the operator's image digest** \- Open a PR against the respective branch replacing the digest with the one from step 1, then merge.  
   1. Digest is updated [here](https://github.com/securesign/policy-controller-operator/blob/main/helm-charts/policy-controller-operator/values.yaml#L19)  
3. **Update the FBC** \- Manually add or update the **bundle** image with the corresponding entry in the FBC using the [opm](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.9/html/cli_tools/opm-cli) tool.

### 

### 

### **Release Process**

The release process mirrors the one used for the RHTAS and MVO operators. At a high level it involves:

1. Creating or updating the release resources (ReleasePlanAdmission, ReleasePlan, and Release).  
2. Getting QE approval for the build.  
3. Applying the resources to the Konflux cluster to initiate the release.

#### **Release Order**

Releases must always be performed in dependency order so that downstream artifacts reference released images:

**policy controller \-\> policy controller operator \-\> FBC images**

This matches the component \-\> operator \-\> FBC pattern used across the other operators.

# MVO

Overview  
The current process for the Model Validation Operator (MVO) release build is almost entirely manual. While the MVO and the Model Transparency CLI are separate entities with independent build processes, we currently bundle them together for convenience.

MVO has migrated from the Python-based model transparency library to the Go-based version, meaning these components can now be released independently if needed.

Model-Transparency  
The Model Transparency konflux project currently consists of a single application with one component. The release process follows a workflow nearly identical to a standard Securesign release, involving a container image bundle and a Python package distribution.

The release starts by capturing a snapshot from a successful push to the `main` branch.

* Create a Pull Request (PR) in the `releases` repository.  
* Follow the existing Securesign release schema, substituting the relevant Model Transparency metadata (image tags, digests, etc.).

The Python package must be released to the Python Package Index (PyPI) simultaneously with the image. We use Hatch to manage the build and publication.

1\. Navigate to the specific commit associated with the release snapshot.  
2\. Open your terminal and export the following environment variables (retrieve the API token from the team Bitwarden):

```
export HATCH_INDEX_USER=__token__
export HATCH_INDEX_AUTH=<your_pypi_token>
```

3\. Run the following commands to package and upload the library:

```
hatch build
hatch publish
```

4\. Once the image and package are successfully published, ensure you create and push a Git tag for the release to maintain version history.

Model-Validation-Operator  
The Model Validation Operator (MVO) application on Konflux consists of three core components: the Agent, the Operator, and the Bundle.

1\. model-validation-operator  
2\. model-validation-operator-agent  
3\. model-validation-operator-bundle

While the post-build stages remain manual, the snapshot generation itself is fully automated. When a push is made to the `main` branch, it triggers a sequential pipeline: the Agent image builds first, which then triggers the Operator build, and finally pipes into the Bundle build.

This automated chain produces a complete release snapshot; however, all subsequent steps, such as preparing the File-Based Catalog (FBC) and final release coordination which currently requires manual intervention.

Once the automated snapshot is generated, the process moves to the FBC repository. This stage is currently manual and involves generating catalog fragments for multiple OpenShift Container Platform (OCP) versions.

Currently, we support OCP versions 4.16 through 4.21. You must manually trigger the build for these versions locally or in your CI environment to ensure the new MVO bundle is correctly indexed.

The final phase of the release cycle involves consolidating all generated artifacts into the Releases repository.

### Releases PR Submission

Once you have collected the FBC snapshots and the MVO component snapshots, you must open a Pull Request in the `releases` repository.

* Follow the standard release resource schema (similar to Securesign).  
* Ensure the snapshot digests for the Operator, Agent, Bundle, and FBC are updated to reflect the new build.  
* Submitting this PR automatically triggers a Staging Run to validate the integration and ensure the components interact correctly in a live environment.

You must manually update the Release Plan Admission on Gitlab to reflect the new versioning. This is where you:

* Update the schema to require the specific tag version for this release cycle.  
* Ensure the plan points to the correct application that passed the staging run etc etc.

  * Set to Konflux Request, and Select whichever release category is relevant.
